Dāyabhāga
(‘Division of estate’)
------------------------------------------
The धर्मशास्त्रस् are the law-books guiding the Hindu society over the centuries. They contain enough material regarding civil as well as criminal topics.
The smṛtis (secondary scriptures), निबन्धस् (digests) and पुराणस् (mythological works) are the main components of these धर्मशास्त्रस्.
One of the topics that has been discussed in great detail in these works is that of division of ancestral property and the rules for इन्हेरितन्चे. On the whole, there has been a broad twofold system prevailing in the country, for nearly a thousand years.
They are: the मिताक्षरा school and the दायभाग school.
The Mitākṣarā or Ṛjumitākṣarā is a magnificent commentary by Vijñaneśvara (12th cent. A. D.) on the ancient work, Yājñavalkya Smṛti. The Dāyabhāga is an independent work, a digest, written by जीमूतवाहन (A. D. 1100). It has a standard commentary called Dāyatattva by रघुनन्दन (A. D. 1510-1580).
The two schools depend almost entirely on these works.
The मिताक्षरा school is the authority accepted all over India except in Bengal (including Bangladesh). However the दायभाग school seems to be a binding authority in Bengal.
According to the मिताक्षरा law, a son, as soon as he was born, became a coparcener (joint owner) with his ड़थेर् in the ancestral property inherited by him. But in the दायभाग system the son did not automatically acquire that right just by birth.
The ड़थेर्, during his life-time, could alienate the property or give it to his children or prepare a will according to his desire. None had the right to question it. If the person passed away without issues, his widow became the owner of that property and not his brothers or other relatives.

Dayānanda सरस्वती, Svāmī
(A. D. 1825-1883)
------------------------------------------
The growth and development of any religion and culture depend to a great extent on the freedom of thought and action, that its votaries enjoy. If Hindu religion and culture have survived the onslaughts of time and change, it is not a little due to this freedom and the reform movements that it engenders. One of the effective and largely successful reform movements of the 19th century is the आर्यसमाज् Movement. Svamī Dayānanda सरस्वती was its founder.
He was born in A. D. 1825, in the small town of Ṭaṅkāra in the Morvi district of Gujarat as the son of Ambāśaṅkar Tivārī and Amṛtābāī. His original name was Mūlaśaṅkara. Being born in an orthodox ब्राह्मण family, he underwent the usual religious sacraments like उपनयन (investiture with the sacred thread) and Vedic studies as also performing religious rites.
The free movement of a little rat on the शिवलिङ्ग on a शिवरात्रि day, became the turning point in his life and in his attitude towards इमगे wओर्स्हिप् as also ritualistic religion. He developed a great abhorrence for the same.
The death of his uncle and a sister made him more introvert and philosophical. One day, when preparations for his मर्रिअगे were going on, he managed to slip away from his होउसे, never to return again.
He started travelling from place to place, in search of a competent गुरु or spiritual teacher. After studying some Vedāntic texts under Svāmī Brahmānanda and परमहṁस Paramānanda, he was ordained into सṁन्यास or monastic life by one Svāmī Pūrṇānanda सरस्वती.
From then onwards he came to be known as Svāmī Dayānanda सरस्वती.
It was actually Svāmī Virajānanda सरस्वती, a blind but erudite and a highly evolved सोउल्, that fulfilled the spiritual aspirations of Dayānanda. After intensive study and training under Him for about three years, Dayānanda set out on his life’s mission as per the directions of his गुरु Virajānanda.
Propagation of the pure Vedic religion based entirely on the Saṁhitās was the main task assigned to him by his गुरु.
Now began his relentless fight against the various unhealthy accretions to the Vedic religion as also the assaults on हिन्दुइस्म् by the Semitic religions. He prepared himself for this onerous task by practising severe austerities for two years in a garden in Agra.
During his ceaseless travels all over the country he mercilessly shattered, through his incisive लोगिच् and vast know-ledge of the वेदस्, the various opinions and practices of the pundits. He successfully roused the religious conscience of the masses. He also reconverted many people who had gone out of the Hindu fold and even gave them the गायत्री-मन्त्र, which he considered as a universal मन्त्र and the common property of all the Hindus.
His insistence on the original Vedic religion as true हिन्दुइस्म्, his call to ignore the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् as a man-made accretion and his stress on the वर्ण system based, not on birth, but on character, earned him a very large following, especially from the deprived sections of the society.
However, his ruthless condemnation of many ritualistic and other practices in the Hindu society based on the secondary scriptures like the पुराणस्, created many enemies for him. His criticism of Islam and Christianity as also his campaign for reconversion of those who had left Hindu religion roused the wrath of the Muslims and the Christians. Several attempts were made against his life.
Dayānanda established the Ārya Samāj at Bombay in 1875 with a creed of 28 principles which he later reduced to 10 in the revision he himself made, in 1877. (See ĀRYASAMĀJ for details.) He passed away in 1883 being poisoned by his own cook, whom he forgave and helped to escape!
By his pure life, fearless and uncompromising adherence to the principles of his conviction, crusades against the forays into the Vedic religion by others and scholarly works like the Satyārthaprakāśa (in Hindi) as also Sanskrit commentaries on some portions of the वेदस्, Dayānanda has carved out a permanent place for himself in हिन्दुइस्म्.
See also SATYĀRTHAPRAKĀŚA.

dayā
(‘compassion’)
------------------------------------------
Showing दया or compassion to all the living creatures and not harming them has been a basic moral discipline enjoined on all, in हिन्दुइस्म्.
The word ‘dayā’ has been defined in various ways:
The desire that arises in one’s heart to mitigate the sufferings of others by putting forth the necessary effort.
The desire to do good to others even as one wishes that others should do towards oneself.
The Devībhāgavatam (1.15.60) des-cribes दया as one of the eight female companions accompanying the देवी (Divine मोथेर्).
The word is also used as an appellation for लक्ष्मी, the consort of विष्णु, since she is the very personification of compassion towards all the living beings who are her children.
Vedānta Deśika (A. D. 1268-1370), the celebrated teacher of the Rāmānuja school, has composed an exquisitely moving hymn called Dayāśatakam on लक्ष्मी as दया.
